At Tlatelolco's Plaza of the Three Cultures, different periods of Mexico City's history can be seen side by side. Low stone ruins belong to the pre-Hispanic city, the colonial Church of Santiago stands nearby, and modern residential buildings rise beyond it.

The square makes it easy to imagine how the capital changed and how new buildings appeared beside old ones. The Church of Saint James, or Santiago, is associated with the city's early Christian history. The square suits both a historical walk and a stop on a pilgrimage route returning from Teotihuacan and Tulpetlac.

Tlaxcala preserves small squares, arcades and churches that offer an accessible introduction to Mexico's early colonial history. The journey here from the capital passes through mountain scenery, and a stroll around town replaces the capital's vast distances with more intimate streets.

Among the city's highlights is the Franciscan Monastery of San Francisco with the Cathedral of the Assumption. The Baroque Basilica of Ocotlán stands nearby. These places bring together architecture and living religious traditions; visitors to the churches should allow time for quiet exploration and prayer.

San Lucas Church and its bell tower stand in Toconao, in Chile's Antofagasta Region. The small church and separate tower form a recognizable part of the village. Here the journey through high-altitude lagoons and the salt flat shifts in scale: local stone architecture and a town square replace wide-open natural landscapes.

The bell tower was entered into Chile's national register of historic monuments by Decree No. 5058 of July 6, 1951. The National Library of Chile also describes the church and bell tower together as one architectural ensemble in Toconao. A visit to both landmarks is part of the stop in the village; access to the interiors and service times should be checked locally.
